claim: Responses of sensory neurons represent stimulus information, but are also influenced by internal state.
source: Responses of sensory neurons represent stimulus information, but are also influenced by internal state.
evidence: This is a general statement about sensory neuron properties that is part of established scientific knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: When monkeys direct their attention to a visual stimulus, the response gain of specific subsets of neurons in visual cortex changes.
source: For example, when monkeys direct their attention to a visual stimulus, the response gain of specific subsets of neurons in visual cortex changes.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the attention literature, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: The functional model reveals four separate time-varying shared modulatory signals.
source: The model reveals four separate time-varying shared modulatory signals, the dominant two of which each target task-relevant neurons in one hemisphere.
evidence: This is a direct result from fitting the model to the experimental data, as shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The dominant two modulatory signals each target task-relevant neurons in one hemisphere.
source: The model reveals four separate time-varying shared modulatory signals, the dominant two of which each target task-relevant neurons in one hemisphere.
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting results shown in Figures 2b-e demonstrating hemispheric specificity and functional selectivity.

claim: In attention-directed conditions, the associated shared modulatory signal decreases in variance.
source: In attention-directed conditions, the associated shared modulatory signal decreases in variance.
evidence: This is directly measured from the fitted model parameters across different attention conditions, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: The decrease in modulator variance provides an interpretable and parsimonious explanation for previous observations that attention reduces variability and noise correlations of sensory neurons.
source: This finding provides an interpretable and parsimonious explanation for previous observations that attention reduces variability and noise correlations of sensory neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results combined with previous empirical observations, as demonstrated in Figures 4-5.

claim: The recovered modulatory signals reflect previous reward.
source: Finally, the recovered modulatory signals reflect previous reward, and are predictive of subsequent choice behavior.
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis of the relationship between modulator values and previous trial outcomes, shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The recovered modulatory signals are predictive of subsequent choice behavior.
source: Finally, the recovered modulatory signals reflect previous reward, and are predictive of subsequent choice behavior.
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical modeling showing modulator values predict hit probability, as shown in Figure 7a.

claim: A substantial portion of neural response variability appears to be due to fluctuations in neurons' excitability, i.e. their gain.
source: Although some of this variability presumably arises from noise in local circuits, a substantial portion appears to be due to fluctuations in neurons' excitability, i.e. their gain (Goris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Goris et al., 2014.

claim: Gain fluctuations in individual neurons are likely not private, but shared across populations.
source: Since this may result from changes in internal states that modulate sensory responses, such as wakefulness, reward, and expectations, or from changes in top-down signals arriving from other cortical areas, it is likely that a significant component of the gain fluctuations in individual neurons are not "private", but shared across populations (Ecker et al., 2014; Schölvinck et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies and represents an inference from those findings.

claim: Shared gain fluctuations could have a crucial impact on sensory computations, depending on their structure.
source: Shared gain fluctuations could have a crucial impact on sensory computations, depending on their structure (Moreno-Bote et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to theoretical work by Moreno-Bote et al., 2014.

claim: When monkeys direct their attention to a visual stimulus, the mean firing rates of specific subsets of visual neurons in striate and extrastriate cortex have been found to increase.
source: When monkeys direct their attention to a visual stimulus, the mean firing rates of specific subsets of visual neurons in striate (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Herrero et al., 2008) and extrastriate cortex (Moran and Desimone, 1985; Treue and Maunsell, 1996; Treue and Maunsell, 1999; Martínez-Trujillo and Treue, 2002; Williford and Maunsell, 2006; Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009) have been found to increase.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Attention acts to increase the gain of selected neurons, thereby increasing the signal-to-noise ratio of sensory representations, and hence improving performance on perceptual tasks.
source: This motivates the hypothesis that, at the level of the population, attention acts to increase the gain of selected neurons, thereby increasing the signal-to-noise ratio of sensory representations, and hence improving performance on perceptual tasks (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Treue and Maunsell, 1996; Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Lee and Maunsell, 2009; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Spatial attention reduces normalized measures of spike count variance.
source: This "classical" view of attention has been augmented by recent observations that spatial attention affects more than mean response: in particular, attention reduces normalized measures of spike count variance, as well as stimulus-conditioned spike count correlations (i.e. "noise correlations") across pairs of neurons (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009; Herrero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Spatial attention reduces stimulus-conditioned spike count correlations (noise correlations) across pairs of neurons.
source: This "classical" view of attention has been augmented by recent observations that spatial attention affects more than mean response: in particular, attention reduces normalized measures of spike count variance, as well as stimulus-conditioned spike count correlations (i.e. "noise correlations") across pairs of neurons (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009; Herrero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Changes in pairwise correlations can arise from changes in direct or indirect couplings between neurons, or changes in common modulatory input.
source: But the origin of these effects is difficult to interpret, as changes in pairwise correlations can arise from changes in direct or indirect couplings between neurons, or changes in common modulatory input (Goris et al., 2014; Ecker et al., 2014; Brody, 1999; Yatsenko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Variability in the attentional signal itself might contribute to spike count variance and correlation.
source: In particular, several groups have suggested that variability in the attentional signal itself might contribute to spike count variance and correlation (Goris et al., 2014; Cohen and Maunsell, 2010; Harris and Thiele, 2011; Ecker et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis suggested by previous work, supported by citations.

claim: The model includes stochastic modulatory signals that alter the gains of targeted subsets of neurons.
source: Here, we develop a functional model for the population activity that accounts for all the above observations. The model includes stochastic modulatory signals that alter the gains of targeted subsets of neurons.
evidence: This describes the structure of the model developed in this study.

claim: The model was fit to spiking data from populations of ~100 neurons in visual area V4, simultaneously recorded from both hemispheres of a macaque monkey.
source: We fit the model to spiking data from populations of ∼100 neurons in visual area V4, simultaneously recorded from both hemispheres of a macaque monkey that was performing a change-detection task under directed spatial attention (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental data used in the study, with citation to the original data source.

claim: The fitted model reveals that the population was predominantly influenced by two independent shared modulatory signals.
source: The resulting fitted model reveals that the population was predominantly influenced by two independent shared modulatory signals, each operating primarily within one hemisphere, and each targeting the neurons most relevant for the task.
evidence: This is a result from fitting the model to the data, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Each modulator operates primarily within one hemisphere.
source: The resulting fitted model reveals that the population was predominantly influenced by two independent shared modulatory signals, each operating primarily within one hemisphere, and each targeting the neurons most relevant for the task.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model fitting results shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: Each modulator targets the neurons most relevant for the task.
source: The resulting fitted model reveals that the population was predominantly influenced by two independent shared modulatory signals, each operating primarily within one hemisphere, and each targeting the neurons most relevant for the task.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation between modulator coupling weights and neural d' values shown in Figure 2d-e.

claim: The statistics of each modulator changed significantly depending on the attentional condition.
source: The statistics of each of these signals changed significantly depending on the attentional condition, with each modulator exhibiting a decrease in variance when the monkey was cued to attend to the stimuli in the corresponding hemifield.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Each modulator exhibits a decrease in variance when the monkey was cued to attend to the stimuli in the corresponding hemifield.
source: The statistics of each of these signals changed significantly depending on the attentional condition, with each modulator exhibiting a decrease in variance when the monkey was cued to attend to the stimuli in the corresponding hemifield.
evidence: This is directly measured from the fitted model parameters, as shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Changes in the statistics of the shared modulatory signals account for the previously-reported decrease in neural variability and noise correlations.
source: Together with the (classical) increases in mean response, these changes in the statistics of the shared modulatory signals account for the previously-reported decrease in neural variability and noise correlations.
evidence: This is demonstrated through model predictions compared to observed data in Figures 4-5.

claim: The inferred modulatory signals are correlated with the monkey's behavioral performance on each trial.
source: Finally, we show that the inferred modulatory signals are correlated with the monkey's behavioral performance on each trial, and are influenced by the reward received on the previous trial.
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The inferred modulatory signals are influenced by the reward received on the previous trial.
source: Finally, we show that the inferred modulatory signals are correlated with the monkey's behavioral performance on each trial, and are influenced by the reward received on the previous trial.
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 7c.

claim: A total of 3004 units were collected and deemed suitable for further analysis over 36 recording days.
source: Over 36 recording days, 3004 units were collected and deemed suitable for further analysis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset size.

claim: Approximately 10^5 presentations of the standard (non-target) stimuli were analyzed.
source: We analyzed spiking responses from these populations to a total of ∼105 presentations of the standard (i.e. non-target) stimuli.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of stimulus presentations analyzed.

claim: The response window was offset by 60 ms to account for stimulus-response latency.
source: We examined the total spike count for each 200 ms stimulus period, offsetting the response window by 60 ms to account for stimulus-response latency (as in Cohen and Maunsell, 2009).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the data analysis, following previous work.

claim: The model assumes that there are K shared time-varying modulators indexed by k.
source: We assume that there are K such modulatory signals, indexed by k.
evidence: This describes a structural assumption of the model.

claim: The net instantaneous firing rate of each neuron is written as rn(t)=fn(s(t))·exp(un·c(t)+vn·d(t)+∑k=1K wn,k·mk(t)).
source:
The net instantaneous firing rate of the neuron is written as:

(1)rn(t)=fn(s(t))·expun·c(t)+vn·d(t)+∑k=1Kwn,k·mk(t)
evidence: This is the mathematical formulation of the model.

claim: The accuracy of model predictions for held-out data improved substantially with the inclusion of each model component.
source: The accuracy of model predictions for these held-out data improved substantially with the inclusion of each model component (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cross-validated log-likelihood scores shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The shared modulators were twice as important as the experimentally-controlled attentional cue signal in making predictions on held-out data.
source: The figure shows that the shared modulators were twice as important as the experimentally-controlled attentional cue signal in making predictions on held-out data.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the improvements in log-likelihood shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The spike count predictions on held-out data improved substantially with the inclusion of two modulators, and showed a modest additional increase for up to four modulators.
source: We found that the spike count predictions on held-out data improved substantially with the inclusion of two modulators, and showed a modest additional increase for up to four modulators.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a comparing models with different numbers of modulators.

claim: Including additional modulators beyond four did not improve predictions.
source: Including additional modulators beyond these did not improve predictions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a where performance plateaus after 4 modulators.

claim: The estimated coupling weights for each modulator clearly identify the hemisphere in which the corresponding neurons reside.
source: First, although the model was not given any information regarding anatomical location or connectivity of the neurons, the estimated coupling weights for each modulator clearly identify the hemisphere in which the corresponding neurons reside (Figure 2b–c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the clustering of weights by hemisphere shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: In a given recording, each modulator had largely positive weights for neurons in one hemisphere and small weights for neurons in the opposite hemisphere.
source: In a given recording, each modulator had largely positive weights for neurons in one hemisphere (indicating that these neurons' gains were being co-modulated by this signal), and small weights for neurons in the opposite hemisphere.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b-c demonstrating hemispheric specificity of modulator weights.

claim: The two hemispheric V4 subpopulations are modulated by two independent signals.
source: Thus, the weight structure of the estimated model suggests that the two hemispheric V4 subpopulations are modulated by two independent signals.
evidence: This is inferred from the hemispheric specificity of the modulator weights shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: The restricted model with enforced hemispheric assignment results in a modest improvement in the quality of model predictions on held-out data.
source: This enforced assignment reduces the number of weight parameters by a factor of two, and results in a modest improvement in the quality of model predictions on held-out data, reaching the level of the 4-modulator model (Figure 2a, grey square).
evidence: This is shown by the grey square in Figure 2a.

claim: The modulators preferentially targeted the most task-informative neurons.
source: Comparison of these values to the modulator coupling weights indicates that the modulators preferentially targeted the most task-informative neurons (r = 0.42; Figure 2d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation between d' and modulator weights shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Units with higher mean firing rates typically had stronger coupling weights to the modulators.
source: One might suspect that some portion of this effect is simply due to firing rate—units with higher mean firing rates typically had stronger coupling weights to the modulators, paralleling previous observations (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009; de la Rocha et al., 2007; Ecker et al., 2010) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The relationship between task informativeness and modulator coupling remains robust even when conditioned on firing rate.
source: But the relationship between task informativeness and modulator coupling remains robust even when conditioned on firing rate (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2e showing the relationship holds within firing rate-matched subpopulations.

claim: The correlation between task informativeness and coupling weights was weaker for the cue signal (r = 0.24) than for the modulators (r = 0.42).
source: Finally, this correlation with functional specificity was weaker for the coupling weights to the cue signal (r = 0.24), and entirely absent from the coupling weights to the slow global drift signal (r < 0.01; Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a direct comparison of correlation coefficients from the data analysis.

claim: The correlation between task informativeness and coupling weights was entirely absent from the slow global drift signal (r < 0.01).
source: Finally, this correlation with functional specificity was weaker for the coupling weights to the cue signal (r = 0.24), and entirely absent from the coupling weights to the slow global drift signal (r < 0.01; Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation coefficient from the data analysis.

claim: When the monkey was cued to attend to one visual hemifield, the shared modulator of the corresponding (contralateral) V4 population had a smaller variance.
source: Here, a clear pattern is evident: when the monkey was cued to attend to one visual hemifield, the shared modulator of the corresponding (contralateral) V4 population had a smaller variance (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the distribution of variance ratios shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The modulators' mean values were unchanged across blocks.
source: The modulators' mean values were unchanged across blocks, as any changes in mean rate are captured by the coupling to the cue signal: 75% of neurons had a positive coupling weight to the cue signal, capturing an increase in their firing rate under cued attention.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting showing how different components capture different aspects of the response.

claim: 75% of neurons had a positive coupling weight to the cue signal.
source: The modulators' mean values were unchanged across blocks, as any changes in mean rate are captured by the coupling to the cue signal: 75% of neurons had a positive coupling weight to the cue signal, capturing an increase in their firing rate under cued attention.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the distribution of cue coupling weights from the data.

claim: Attention both increases and stabilizes the time-varying gain of the corresponding neural population.
source: Thus, in general, attention both increases and stabilizes the time-varying gain of the corresponding neural population.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of increased mean (via cue weights) and decreased variance (of modulators) shown in Figure 3.

claim: Averaged across days and hemispheres, cued attention reduces modulator variance by 23%.
source: Averaged across days and hemispheres, cued attention reduces modulator variance by 23%.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 3b and represents a summary statistic from the data.

claim: A decrease in modulator variance leads to a reduction in the spike count variance of each neuron, without a large change in their mean firing rates.
source: A decrease in the variance of this shared signal leads to a reduction in the spike count variance of each neuron, without a large change in their mean firing rates (Goris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citation to previous work and demonstrated in simulation in Figure 4b.

claim: A decrease in modulator variance causes a decrease in the spike-count correlation of neuron pairs.
source: Moreover, since both neurons are coupled to the same modulatory signal, the decrease in modulator variance also causes a decrease in the spike-count correlation of the pair.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction demonstrated in simulation in Figure 4b.

claim: The magnitudes of the Fano factors and noise correlations increase with the magnitude of the weights with which the neurons are coupled to the hemispheric modulators.
source: The model thus makes a very specific prediction: the magnitudes of the Fano factors and noise correlations should increase with the magnitude of the weights with which the neurons are coupled to the hemispheric modulators. We find that this prediction is clearly borne out by the data (Figure 5a), and is robust when controlled for firing rate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a model prediction that is confirmed by the data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Neurons that are more strongly coupled to the modulators exhibit a larger attention-induced reduction in Fano factor and noise correlation.
source: In addition, since the modulator variance decreases under cued attention, the model predicts that those neurons that are more strongly coupled should exhibit a larger attention-induced reduction in these measures. This effect is also apparent in the data (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a model prediction confirmed by the data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The model accounts for 62% of the cue-induced reduction in Fano factor.
source: The model accounts for 62% of the cue-induced reduction in Fano factor, and 71% of the reduction in noise correlation.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 5b and represents a quantitative comparison between model predictions and data.

claim: The model accounts for 71% of the reduction in noise correlation.
source: The model accounts for 62% of the cue-induced reduction in Fano factor, and 71% of the reduction in noise correlation.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 5b and represents a quantitative comparison between model predictions and data.

claim: Neurons which were most strongly coupled to the modulators were also most strongly coupled to the cue signal.
source: We did observe that neurons which were most strongly coupled to the modulators were also most strongly coupled to the cue signal (Figure 5c; even when controlled for firing rate Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c demonstrating a correlation between cue and modulator weights.

claim: The correlation between the coupling weights to the cue signal and the coupling weights to the hemispheric modulator was modest (Spearman ρ = 0.26).
source: But overall, the correlation between the coupling weights to the cue signal and the coupling weights to the hemispheric modulator was modest (Spearman ρ = 0.26).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation coefficient from the data analysis.

claim: A restricted model in which cue and modulator signals had identical coupling weights reduced predictive log-likelihood performance by 20%.
source: We fit a restricted model in which these two signals had identical coupling weights, and found that the predictive (log-likelihood) performance was reduced by 20%.
evidence: This is a result from fitting an alternative model to test whether cue and modulator effects are identical.

claim: The modulator weights were predictive of the Fano factor and noise correlation effects (correlations ρ > 0.3), while the cue weights were much less so (ρ < 0.1).
source: Moreover, while the modulator weights were predictive of the Fano factor and noise correlation effects (as shown in Figure 5a; correlations ρ > 0.3), the cue weights were much less so (ρ < 0.1).
evidence: This is a comparison of correlation coefficients from the data analysis.

claim: The effects of the cue and of the inferred hemispheric modulator overlap but are not identical, suggesting that they arise (at least in part) from distinct sources.
source: Thus, although the effects of the cue and of the inferred hemispheric modulator overlap, they are not identical, suggesting that they arise (at least in part) from distinct sources.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the partial correlation between cue and modulator weights and the performance of restricted models.

claim: The two hemispheres' time-varying modulator values were almost completely uncorrelated (r = 0.03).
source: First, the two hemispheres' time-varying modulator values were almost completely uncorrelated (Figure 6a; r = 0.03).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a and represents a direct measurement from the inferred modulator values.

claim: The modulators exhibited correlations over successive stimulus presentations, indicating that gain fluctuations can persist over time scales of seconds.
source: Second, the modulators exhibited correlations over successive stimulus presentations (Figure 6b), indicating that gain fluctuations can persist over time scales of seconds.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6b demonstrating temporal autocorrelation of the modulators.

claim: The shared modulators had only weak effects during response onsets, and exerted their influence on neural gain primarily during the sustained response period.
source: We found that the shared modulators had only weak effects during response onsets, and exerted their influence on neural gain primarily during the sustained response period (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6c demonstrating the temporal profile of modulator effects within each stimulus presentation.

claim: The temporal profile of modulators is consistent with previous reports that attentional effects on firing rates (and Fano factors) are greater during sustained periods.
source: This property of the modulators is consistent with previous reports that attentional effects on firing rates (and Fano factors) are greater during sustained periods (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009;Mitchell et al., 2009, and with more general observations that network behavior is less affected by context or state during onset transients (Churchland, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to previous observations, supported by citations.

claim: An increase in the cued modulator preceded an increased detection probability for cued targets.
source: As may be expected, changes in each hemispheric modulator predicted performance changes for their associated targets: an increase in the cued modulator preceded an increased detection probability for cued targets; while an increase in the opposite modulator preceded higher detection probabilities for opposite targets (top left and bottom right of Figure 7a; see Figure 7—figure supplement 1a for full psychometrics).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a demonstrating the relationship between modulator values and behavioral performance.

claim: An increase in the opposite modulator preceded higher detection probabilities for opposite targets.
source: As may be expected, changes in each hemispheric modulator predicted performance changes for their associated targets: an increase in the cued modulator preceded an increased detection probability for cued targets; while an increase in the opposite modulator preceded higher detection probabilities for opposite targets (top left and bottom right of Figure 7a; see Figure 7—figure supplement 1a for full psychometrics).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a demonstrating the relationship between modulator values and behavioral performance.

claim: The effect of modulators on behavior is substantially stronger for the opposite side than the cued side.
source: Suprisingly, this effect is substantially stronger for the opposite side.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the magnitudes of effects shown in Figure 7a.

claim: An increase in one side's modulator predicted a decrease in detection probability on the other side.
source: In addition to this modulator-driven improvement in detection probabilities, we also uncovered a striking deficit in performance on the opposite side. Specifically, an increase in one side's modulator predicted a decrease in detection probability on the other side (top right and bottom left of Figure 7a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a demonstrating competitive effects of modulators on behavior.

claim: The competitive pattern of modulator effects on behavior likely reflects the competitive structure of the task, which requires the animal to make comparisons between the represented stimuli in both hemispheres.
source: This is not due to anti-correlation of the two modulators (they are nearly uncorrelated; Figure 6a). Rather, this pattern likely reflects the competitive structure of the task, which requires the animal to make comparisons between the represented stimuli in both hemispheres.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the observed competitive effects.

claim: After receiving a reward for correctly identifying a cued target, monkeys were more likely to score a hit for a cued target on the next trial.
source: The monkeys in this task also exhibit a serial dependence: after receiving a reward for correctly identifying a cued target, they were more likely to score a hit for a cued target, and a miss for an opposite target, on the next trial.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b demonstrating sequential effects in behavior.

claim: After receiving a reward for correctly identifying a cued target, monkeys were more likely to score a miss for an opposite target on the next trial.
source: The monkeys in this task also exhibit a serial dependence: after receiving a reward for correctly identifying a cued target, they were more likely to score a hit for a cued target, and a miss for an opposite target, on the next trial.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b demonstrating sequential effects in behavior.

claim: After receiving a reward for correctly identifying an opposite target, monkeys were substantially more likely to score a hit for an opposite target on the next trial.
source: Conversely, after receiving a reward for correctly identifying an opposite target, on the next trial they are substantially more likely to score a hit for an opposite target, and a miss for a cued target (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b demonstrating sequential effects in behavior.

claim: After receiving a reward for correctly identifying an opposite target, monkeys were more likely to score a miss for a cued target on the next trial.
source: Conversely, after receiving a reward for correctly identifying an opposite target, on the next trial they are substantially more likely to score a hit for an opposite target, and a miss for a cued target (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b demonstrating sequential effects in behavior.

claim: A hit on a cued target biased the two modulators on the subsequent trial to shift in favor of the cued population.
source: A hit (and thus, a reward) on a cued target biased the two modulators on the subsequent trial to shift in favor of the cued population, while a hit on the opposite target biased the two modulators on the subsequent trial to shift in favor of the opposite population (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7c demonstrating the effect of previous reward on modulator values.

claim: A hit on the opposite target biased the two modulators on the subsequent trial to shift in favor of the opposite population.
source: A hit (and thus, a reward) on a cued target biased the two modulators on the subsequent trial to shift in favor of the cued population, while a hit on the opposite target biased the two modulators on the subsequent trial to shift in favor of the opposite population (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7c demonstrating the effect of previous reward on modulator values.

claim: Only 5–10% of the total serial dependence can be explained through the V4 modulators.
source: However, we note that only 5–10% of the total serial dependence can be explained through the V4 modulators (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b, representing a quantitative comparison.

claim: Reward must also induce additional biases in the activity of downstream neurons involved in the animals' decisions.
source: We conclude that reward must also induce additional biases in the activity of downstream neurons involved in the animals' decisions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that V4 modulators only partially explain behavioral serial dependence.

claim: The inferred signals that modulate neural gain in V4 populations are intimately connected with the monkey's previous and subsequent behaviors.
source: In summary, we found that the inferred signals that modulate neural gain in V4 populations are intimately connected with the monkey's previous and subsequent behaviors.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Attention reduces the correlation between spiking and concurrent slow fluctuations in local field potential (LFP).
source: Specifically, attention reduces the correlation between spiking and concurrent slow fluctuations in local field potential (LFP) (Fries et al., 2001), which themselves are reduced in power (Fries et al., 2001; Siegel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: LFP fluctuations are reduced in power under attention.
source: Specifically, attention reduces the correlation between spiking and concurrent slow fluctuations in local field potential (LFP) (Fries et al., 2001), which themselves are reduced in power (Fries et al., 2001; Siegel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: The patterns of response variability seen throughout visual cortex show signatures of multiplicative, rather than additive noise.
source: The multiplicative nature of this interaction is broadly consistent with the patterns of response variability seen throughout visual cortex, which show signatures of multiplicative, rather than additive noise (Goris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Goris et al., 2014.

claim: The patterns of response variance along the adaptation axis are consistent with the multiplicative hypothesis.
source: Nevertheless, the modest reduction in firing rates arising from adaptation to repeated presentations of the standard stimuli provides some opportunity to examine this question. We find that the patterns of response variance along this axis are indeed consistent with the multiplicative hypothesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 analyzing variance as a function of firing rate.

claim: Pairs of neurons within the same hemisphere whose responses provide evidence for opposite behavioral choices can exhibit increased noise correlations under spatial attention.
source: One of us recently reported that pairs of neurons within the same hemisphere whose responses provide evidence for opposite behavioral choices can exhibit increased noise correlations under spatial attention (Ruff and Cohen, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Ruff and Cohen, 2014.

claim: The model does not account for all of the observed cue-dependent changes in variability.
source: However, the model does not account for all of the observed cue-dependent changes in variability (Figure 5b), suggesting that the model structure (e.g. Poisson spiking, with rate modulated by an exponentiated sum of shared signals) is too restricted to capture the full extent of the effects.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b where model predictions do not fully match observed changes.

claim: The dimensionality and structure of the estimated modulators are limited by the experiment itself.
source: Moreover, the dimensionality and structure of the estimated modulators are limited by the experiment itself (Gao and Ganguli, 2015), and thus cannot be taken as a complete account of modulatory activity in V4.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the study, supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: A primary contribution of this work is to show that the patterns of neural variability in a visual cortical population during this attentional task are dominated by a few internal signals.
source: In this respect, a primary contribution of our work is to show that the patterns of neural variability in a visual cortical population during this attentional task are dominated by a few internal signals.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the main finding of the study.

claim: Cholinergic input has a multiplicative and hemispherically-specific effect on neurons in macaque visual cortex.
source: One potential top-down biological substrate is cholinergic input, which has a multiplicative (Disney et al., 2007) and hemispherically-specific (Mesulam et al., 1983) effect on neurons in macaque visual cortex, and is known to be enhanced under attention (Herrero et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: In area V1, cholinergic input mediates attention-dependent increases in mean firing rate, but not changes in response variance or noise correlations.
source: However, it has recently been shown that in area V1, cholinergic input mediates attention-dependent increases in mean firing rate, but not changes in response variance or noise correlations, which appear to depend on NMDA receptors (Herrero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work by Herrero et al., 2013.

claim: The attention-mediated increase and stabilization of gain in area V4 might arise from two separate mechanisms.
source: Consistent with these findings, our model suggests that the attention-mediated increase and stabilization of gain in area V4 might arise from two separate mechanisms: the estimated coupling weights associated with the cue and modulator signals are similar but not identical (Figure 5c), and when they are forced to be identical, model predictions worsen.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results and comparison with previous findings.

claim: The gain fluctuations specifically target those neurons relevant to the task.
source: The gain fluctuations we uncover do not affect every neuron in the population, but specifically target those neurons relevant to the task (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8b demonstrating that gain variability is higher for task-relevant neurons.

claim: While modulator variance decreases under attention, it remains larger for the task-relevant neurons.
source: And while their variance certainly decreases under attention, it remains a puzzle why these gain fluctuations are there at all, given that they are nearly absent from the task-irrelevant neurons (which, presumably, would be relevant for different tasks).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8b and represents an observation that challenges the simple noise interpretation.

claim: Modulator fluctuations have a direct and immediate effect on the perceptual decisions made by the animal.
source: However, this does not appear to be the case: modulator fluctuations have a direct and immediate effect on the perceptual decisions made by the animal (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a demonstrating the relationship between modulator values and behavioral performance.

claim: Only units with mean firing rates greater than 0.5 spikes/s were included in the analysis.
source: We only included data from units with mean firing rates greater than 0.5 spikes/s.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data inclusion criteria.

claim: For each recording day, 20% of the spike count observations were set aside as a test set for cross-validation.
source: For each stimulus presentation, a random subset of 20% of the spike count observations were set aside as a test set.
evidence: This describes the cross-validation procedure used in the study.
